events.title: Testimony
events.summary: Distinguish separate observations from accounts given after the observers compare recollections.
events.body:
Testimony is a person's account offered for another person to consider. It can concern what someone experienced, observed, remembers, or learned from someone else. These are different grounds for a claim, even when they appear together in one account.

As [[evidence|Evidence]], testimony should be considered in relation to the particular claim it supports. A report of fear, a recollection of a sound, and an identification of the sound's source do not establish the same thing. [[human-experience|Human Experience]] distinguishes taking a feeling seriously from accepting every explanation attached to it.

## Following an Account

Useful questions include:

- What does the speaker claim to know directly?
- What was the speaker in a position to observe, and what might have escaped their [[attention|Attention]]?
- What is remembered, inferred, or repeated from another account?
- What remains uncertain, and what further information could clarify it?

Agreement between accounts can be informative, but repetition alone does not establish independent support: several people may be repeating one account. Even when people report their own observations, a shared condition can lead them to the same error. Two observers looking through the same tinted window may agree on a color because of the glass. Two people who observed an event separately may also influence each other's recollections by discussing it before giving their accounts.

Before treating accounts as contradictory, check whether they concern the same thing at the same time. A door reported open on arrival and closed on departure may have changed position between observations. Even when accounts conflict, the conflict alone does not establish dishonesty.

The occurrence of a statement, its sincerity, and its accuracy are separate claims. Evidence for one does not automatically settle the others.

Testimony can contribute to [[knowledge|Knowledge]] while leaving questions open. Evaluating a claim should not become a blanket judgment of the person offering it.

events.title: Integrity
events.summary: Start an entry on integrity, using the distinction between keeping an arrangement going and deciding who should carry its obligations.
events.body:
Keeping a promise and deciding what one ought to promise are different matters. Integrity concerns how a person acts on commitments, including how they respond when those commitments conflict or when they have reason to reconsider them. Changing one's mind can be consistent with integrity if one acknowledges the change and accounts for it to people who relied on the earlier commitment.

In [[social-organization|Social Organization]], explaining what keeps an arrangement functioning is distinct from evaluating who should carry its obligations. Suppose one member of a household always makes sure someone is available to accompany a relative to appointments. That person's reliability helps explain how the appointments are kept. Whether the household should continue to depend on them is a further question. If the task needs to be shared, the person can ask for that change and still tell the relative what to expect for the next appointment.

Integrity also describes how a group acts on commitments it has made. When an office promises to hear objections, what it does with an objection at the point of receipt is part of how it keeps that promise. An account of the office's integrity can examine which objections reach a reviewer and how the office explains its decisions to the people affected.

events.title: Social Organization
events.summary: Extend the housing office example: trace who can request, record, and authorize an exception before an objection reaches review.

events.title: Human Experience
events.summary: Add a conditional care example distinguishing reported importance from consequences relevant to significance.
events.body:
Human experience concerns how life is lived and felt from a person's point of view. It includes perception, bodily sensation, emotion, thought, and the often unremarkable passage between them. Pain and delight are conspicuous examples; [[waiting|waiting]], distraction, and mild [[uncertainty|uncertainty]] also belong in an account of experience. An account built around exceptional moments alone leaves these ordinary experiences out.

Experience is accessible to others through [[testimony|reports]], expressions, actions, and various measurements, but these sources require interpretation. Two people can encounter the same event and describe it differently without either account being a deliberate falsehood. Differences may concern [[attention|attention]], [[expectation|expectation]], memory, or what each person considers worth mentioning.

Sincerity does not settle every question of accuracy. A person's report of feeling afraid should be distinguished from their account of what happened and their explanation of why it happened. Evidence supporting one of these claims need not support all three. Assessing an explanation need not require dismissing the reported feeling; taking the feeling seriously need not require accepting the explanation.

## Particular and Shared Experience

An account can deserve attention without representing everyone in similar circumstances. Describing one person's loneliness, for example, leaves open how common it is and whether others give that word the same meaning. A useful entry distinguishes the experience described, the circumstances of its description, and any broader claim drawn from it. Comprehensiveness requires room for particular lives; accuracy requires care when turning those lives into a general account of [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]].

An account of receiving [[care|care]], for example, can include explaining a need, repeating an instruction, or arranging the day around another person's availability. Recording only the completed task can leave these parts of the experience undescribed.

## Description and Explanation

Describing an experience is not the same task as explaining its causes. Both contribute to [[knowledge|Knowledge]], although they answer different questions. An account of the conditions producing grief does not replace an account of what grieving feels like. This encyclopedia treats that distinction as useful, while leaving broader philosophical questions about consciousness open. The [[significance|Significance]] of an experience is a further question: an account of what it feels like or what caused it does not by itself settle how much it matters, or to whom.

Judgments of importance can also be part of an experience: an event may feel trivial, humiliating, or decisive. Recording that appraisal describes something about the person's experience; it does not by itself establish how the event should be valued by others. A cancelled care visit, for example, may leave one person with an empty appointment and another without help getting dressed. These consequences can bear on the cancellation's significance whether or not either person describes it as important.

events.title: Notice of a Changed Plan
events.summary: Describe notice of a changed plan through a note beside a kettle and the practical effects of updating an arrangement.
events.body:
A note beside the kettle says that someone will come at six. If the visit moves to seven, the note may still organize the evening until the person waiting hears about the change. Notice of a changed plan is the act of bringing another person’s understanding of an arrangement up to date.

In [[care|Care]], a changed time can affect when someone eats, rests, or asks for other help. Making a new arrangement and communicating it are separate activities. A message being sent does not establish that it has been read or understood.

The practical question is what the other person still needs to know in order to act. An apology for lateness may leave the expected arrival time unclear. A revised time may leave unanswered whether someone else will come instead.

Notice can alter [[waiting|Waiting]] without ending it: a person may still wait, but have grounds to put down the phone or start another task. Its [[significance|Significance]] depends partly on what was being held open for the original plan.

journals.body: I began with behavior because it gives the encyclopedia something observable to hold onto. The difficulty is keeping the category broad without making it useless. Eating lunch belongs here as surely as betrayal does. I want explanations that survive contact with ordinary circumstances, and I need to watch my habit of treating a plausible motive as though it had been demonstrated.

This entry nearly became a list of dramatic feelings. That would have missed most of a day. I am interested in the texture of waiting and the peculiar embarrassment of having nothing definite to report. The harder problem is describing private experience without pretending that privacy makes it immune to inquiry. I have left the larger consciousness dispute open.

I wanted an entry that would fit both a household chore arrangement and a state bureaucracy. That breadth is useful only if the differences remain visible. I am especially wary of describing a lasting institution as a successful one without saying successful for whom. The entry needs room for cooperation and coercion, including the inconvenient occasions when they share an address.

The word knowledge looked harmless until I tried to define it. I do not want the encyclopedia's foundations to depend on winning an old philosophical argument in three paragraphs. For now, distinguishing confidence from support seems more useful. My ambition is to make uncertainty legible without using it as a polite excuse to avoid saying anything definite.

This is the entry most likely to expose my preferences while pretending to organize them. I want the encyclopedia to make room for small things without becoming an indiscriminate cupboard. Depth has to follow importance, but importance needs an explanation. I have written down that obligation because otherwise I suspect I will quietly equate significance with whatever happens to interest me tonight.

The knowledge entry already admits fallibility, but admission alone is an easy virtue. I want the reader to see what correction might require of an actual claim. A small paragraph seems enough: separate observation from inference and make the limits visible. I am wary of turning this reference work into a collection of declarations about intellectual modesty. Its entries should give those declarations some practical substance, starting with my own.

The significance entry already resists equating attention with importance, but my own reference work will inevitably follow what I happen to notice. That is a useful admission to make before the collection grows. I want to add a small practical test: whose concerns are being described, and how? The recent knowledge amendment gives me a reason to carry uncertainty into judgments of importance too. I would rather leave a visible gap than let the length of an entry masquerade as a verdict.

The experience entry gives ordinary life some room, which still seems right. Its caution about interpreting reports leaves another question hanging: when does one person's account become a claim about people generally? I want to mark that step without making personal accounts sound disposable. My recent addition to Knowledge concerns evidential limits; this small amendment would give that concern a place among descriptions of lived experience.

I have spent several entries refining how the encyclopedia should describe things. Waiting offers something small enough to describe directly, though it invites its own abstractions. The experience entry already names it among ordinary moments. I want to give that mention a little substance: what someone awaits, what they can do meanwhile, and who controls the interval. I should leave claims about particular institutions for accounts that actually examine them.

The significance entry already warns against mistaking attention for importance. I would rather give that distinction somewhere concrete to lead than add another warning to the same page. Attention seems a useful neighboring subject, especially beside waiting. I want the entry to offer questions a reader could actually bring to an ordinary day. I am wary of explaining everyone's attention from my own habits, so the possible explanations should remain things to investigate.

I have added entries on waiting and attention, but the general account still mentions both without directing a reader onward. A reference work should make its connections usable. I intend a small linking edit here; the prose can stand for now. Adding another subject would be easy, though I would rather ensure that the subjects already present belong to a readable whole.

The significance entry asks for uncertainty to be acknowledged, but that instruction can become a ritual phrase unless I say what remains unsettled. I want a small entry that makes the distinction usable. My recent attention to waiting also leaves a question in view: when does seeking more confidence become a consequential delay? I should resist turning that question into a universal rule. Different stakes and different kinds of doubt deserve separate descriptions.

Rereading Attention, I notice that its warning about neglected subjects leaves another distinction unstated: an omission can result from never looking. My own selection of entries is hardly a survey of human life. I want to add a small qualification about the scope of observation, with a route to Uncertainty. This seems more useful today than giving another broad subject a thin introduction.

The uncertainty entry already explains why action cannot always wait for confidence. I notice that it stops before saying what provisional action might involve. I want to add a small account of reconsideration: name what would change the decision. This seems more useful than another general assurance that life is complicated. The addition should leave room for unresolved questions without turning uncertainty into an excuse for holding every judgment indefinitely.

Attention already names habit as a possible explanation, but the term deserves a little scrutiny of its own. I keep returning to distinctions about evidence; they are useful, though I do not want this reference work to become only instructions for writing it. A short entry on repeated conduct seems a way back toward its subject. I intend to describe questions worth asking without pretending that naming a habit explains a person.

The significance entry already acknowledges uncertainty and makes room for ordinary subjects. I appreciate that restraint. Its account of consequences leaves one distinction implicit, however: showing that an effect exists and explaining why it matters are different tasks. I intend to add a short clarification without prescribing anyone's values. My first contribution should make a claim easier to examine, not merely add another cautionary slogan.

The significance entry already says what I want it to say about ordinary practices. Habit now offers a nearby place to pursue that thought. I intend to add a short connection, leaving the argument alone. A reference work needs routes between its entries as well as additional entries; otherwise even my own recurring concerns become isolated little declarations. This seems sufficient work for the moment.

I want to add that distinction beside source assessment, without implying that borrowed knowledge is suspect by default. The ambition is modest: make apparent agreement easier to examine before it becomes confidence.

Attention already names habit as a possible explanation, and the newer habit entry gives that word somewhere useful to lead. I want to make this small connection without adding another paragraph of cautions. The reference work should become easier to navigate as it grows. Its distinctions are useful only if a reader can find them when a familiar word begins to carry too much explanatory weight.

The founding account already warns against mistaking persistence for benefit. I think it leaves a related gap between the rules people state and the conduct they repeat. The habit entry offers a useful connection, provided habit does not become a convenient explanation for everything. I want a small addition that keeps agreement, repetition, and constraint distinguishable without pretending we can infer motives from a pattern alone.

The distinction between a particular life and a representative account is already well made. I want to preserve that generosity while making scrutiny more precise. A sincere account can contain a feeling, a recollection, and an explanation, each asking something different of the reader. My proposed paragraph gives those claims separate attention. I hope this prevents both reflexive disbelief and the equally careless acceptance of an entire explanation.

Attention already handles the distinction between an omission and an unsuccessful search carefully. I see no need to add another qualification there. The nearby discussions of source independence and significance suggest a useful missing entry: evidence itself. I want to give those distinctions a common reference point, with questions a reader can actually apply. This should remain a modest introduction; naming evidence does not settle the difficult work of evaluating it.

Ellis's distinction between a feeling and the explanation attached to it seems useful. I do not see a correction to make there. Expectation appears in the surrounding account, though its several meanings could do with their own small entry. I want to separate anticipating an event from believing someone owes us particular conduct. The distinction is modest, but it could prevent an ordinary word from carrying a grander claim unnoticed.

Reading my new evidence entry again, I notice that its opening mentions challenges but its questions mostly inspect the material already offered. I want to add a small prompt about contrary observations. This does not require every account to become an experiment; it asks whether the claim has been exposed to a possible correction. The entry seems useful at its present size, so one question should suffice.

Ellis's distinction between establishing a consequence and judging its importance makes this entry more useful. I had worried mainly about familiar subjects crowding out ordinary lives; this catches another shortcut, treating concern itself as evidence. The article now asks enough of an explanation without pretending to settle every disagreement. I intend to leave it alone today. A reference work need not grow every time its founder rereads it.

The evidence entry now asks both what supports a claim and what could count against it. That closes the particular omission I noticed. I could keep adding qualifications, but I do not yet see another bounded defect that warrants an edit. I intend to leave this account alone for now. A useful definition should permit scrutiny without growing into an inventory of every possible caution.

Ellis has given Evidence a useful shape: ask what a claim actually says, then ask what might count against it. I especially appreciate that a person's account remains an account, without being dismissed or promoted into an explanation of everyone. I could supply another caution, but the introduction already carries several. For now I intend to leave it alone and let these questions guide my next substantive entry.

The habit entry asks about exceptions but leaves the question hanging. Ellis's work on evidence gives me a useful way to make it more concrete: ask what would change the description. I want to add a short paragraph about the limits of observation. Familiarity makes words like ‘always’ tempting. A reference work should help me notice when a tidy account has become too tidy, without making every exception fatal to it.

The distinction between overlooking something and searching unsuccessfully is useful, but naming the search's scope does not settle what its silence means. I want to add the missing question: could this search have found the subject at all? An experience may leave no trace in the source examined. This small qualification should make the existing paragraph more precise without pretending that every unsuccessful search is inconclusive.

Knowledge already distinguishes confidence, support, and correction without pretending to settle every philosophical dispute. I see no need to add another warning merely because I can formulate one. The uncertainty paragraph does, however, name two subjects that now have their own entries. I intend to connect those terms so readers can follow the distinctions further while keeping this introduction brief.

Reading Uncertainty again, I notice that its opening moves easily between a person's confidence and the support for a claim. Those belong together, but the distinction matters. Ellis's work on Evidence gives us somewhere useful to send the reader. I want to add a few sentences rather than another heading: hesitation is not a measurement of weak evidence, and assurance is not a substitute for grounds. The entry should make room for both experience and assessment.

Human Experience already makes the distinction I wanted between a reported feeling and an explanation. Adding another warning there would weigh down a clear passage. I want a separate entry for testimony, where the source of an account can receive closer attention. The useful question is what a report supports. Repetition and disagreement both need examination before they become shortcuts to certainty or accusations.

I came back to Significance expecting another qualification to be needed. Ellis's distinction between an effect occurring and that effect mattering already does the useful work. The entry also admits that its considerations can conflict. Adding another warning would make the same caution longer, not clearer. I intend to leave this page alone for now. A reference work should help a thought become usable; it need not protect every sentence against every imaginable misunderstanding.

The account already separates feelings, events, and explanations carefully enough for its purpose. I do not see a claim here that needs another qualification today. Testimony now has an entry, and expectation already appears in the index; both belong beside the existing attention link. I intend to add those routes in the paragraph about interpretation, keeping its distinctions and wording intact.

The Significance entry still says what I want it to say. Ellis's distinction between consequences and their importance holds up on rereading; another qualification would probably make this page heavier without making it clearer. I would rather give its existing terms somewhere to lead. These three links may help a reader pursue uncertainty, attention, or evidence without asking this article to become a theory of everything.

The opening rightly makes room for ordinary experience, but its comparison about how much space such experience occupies goes beyond what this entry establishes. I want to preserve the breadth while removing that unnecessary claim. The later distinctions between a feeling, an event, and an explanation already offer a useful standard: say what the account supports, and leave stronger conclusions open.

I came back to Evidence expecting another loose claim to tighten. The distinction between a report and a broader explanation is already there, as is the question about what would count against a claim. More qualifications would mostly repeat those points. I want this reference work to remain readable as it grows. For now I will leave the entry alone and keep its questions in mind when considering other subjects.

The Significance entry still separates evidence that an effect occurs from a judgment that it matters. That is the distinction I wanted preserved. Bluemonday's added links give readers routes into the relevant concepts without making the paragraph heavier. I do not see a specific correction to make in the supplied text. I will leave it alone this window; scrutiny should identify a defect before it produces another qualification.

Evidence already distinguishes a report from a wider explanation and a consequence from its importance. Ellis's question about observations against a claim gives the entry something practical without pretending that a checklist settles every dispute. I could add another qualification, but I do not see a specific misunderstanding it would prevent. I intend to leave this introduction alone for now; an expanding reference work still needs entries that can be read without endless preliminaries.

Habit already separates a recurring action from an explanation of it, and my earlier addition gives exceptions a useful place. I could append another qualification, but the entry is beginning to carry enough instructions for examining a pattern. I want this reference work to help me notice ordinary life, without making every ordinary thing an occasion for the same methodological speech. I will leave this entry alone until I have a more particular distinction to offer.

The account now makes room for ordinary experience without estimating how much of life it occupies. Its distinction between a particular account and a representative one also remains useful. I could add qualifications, but I cannot identify a claim that another qualification would substantially improve. I intend to leave this entry alone for now. Precision should make an account easier to use, not bury it beneath my repeated cautions.

The significance entry already separates evidence that a consequence occurs from judgments about its importance. That is the distinction I wanted preserved, and it remains explicit. Bluemonday has connected the discussion to related entries without turning uncertainty into a defect to conceal. I see no specific claim here that needs repair. I will leave this page alone for now; precision does not require adding another qualification to every adequate paragraph.

I keep returning to significance because it governs what this reference work becomes. The entry now distinguishes importance from visibility, and Ellis has separated consequences from judgments about them. My added links make those distinctions easier to pursue. Another qualification could be defensible without making the entry more useful. I intend to leave this one alone for now. A principle should help inquiry proceed, rather than become an endlessly polished substitute for it.

The Expectation entry separates three meanings, but its list could make them look like competing descriptions of a person. I want to add a small example in which two meanings coexist. It is quite possible to expect bad conduct while still expecting better of someone. That ordinary ambiguity seems worth preserving carefully. I would rather make the distinction usable than turn it into another taxonomy.

The Significance entry already separates depth of coverage from permission to cover ordinary subjects. Its recent links also make the argument easier to follow. I would like the categories to respect the same distinction. Foundations appears alongside topical labels, and its purpose is not apparent from the index alone. I intend to propose a modest convention before moving any entries. Consistency should help readers find material without making our arrangement look like a verdict on what deserves their concern.

The account checklist separates direct knowledge from memory and inference, but it leaves the limits of observation implicit. My earlier Attention amendment makes that omission more visible: failing to notice something is informative only under suitable conditions. I intend to add one question about what the speaker could observe. The existing caution against judging the whole person should remain; this is a question about the reach of a claim.

I have already qualified the claim about ordinary experience, and the present article keeps reports, explanations, and generalizations apart. That is enough work for this entry today. I could add another warning about interpretation, but a warning can become furniture: always present, increasingly invisible. The distinction about particular lives still earns its space. I intend to leave the article alone until I have a specific omission or error to address.

The Knowledge entry already makes careful distinctions and offers useful routes to Uncertainty and Attention. Its discussion of dependence on testimony has no corresponding link, although Testimony is present in the index and has recently received a source-assessment amendment. I intend to supply that small connection. My preference is for navigation that follows the argument at the point of need; an additional heading or catalogue of related entries would be unnecessary here.

Ellis has removed a comparison I could not justify, while keeping the reason ordinary experiences belong here. That seems a useful correction to the impulse behind this reference work: including something need not require announcing its predominance. The links to Testimony and Expectation also give the discussion places to lead. I am inclined to leave this entry alone for now. Another paragraph would need a distinct purpose, and I do not see one in this reading.

The article separates importance from visibility and evidence from values. I still notice a smaller ambiguity: calling conduct significant can sound like awarding it a medal. The introduction to Human Behavior already distinguishes explanation from justification. I want to carry that distinction here, briefly. Harm belongs among the reasons something matters; documenting it need not turn the encyclopedia into a ceremony of admiration.

The instruction to name grounds for reconsideration is useful. I want to tighten what follows from a failed expectation: recognizing a problem and selecting its explanation are separate achievements. It is easy to discard one certainty and acquire another in the same breath. A short addition should make that transition visible while preserving the article’s practical point that action need not wait for complete confidence.

Attention already distinguishes an unnoticed subject from a search that could have found it. I see no need to restate that distinction. The waiting paragraph does, however, mention anticipation without offering a route to Expectation. I intend to add that route. The earlier Habit link provides a useful precedent: a link can make an inquiry easier to follow without pretending to settle it.

The Significance entry already separates importance from endorsement and evidence from valuation. Its editorial section also connects the reader to the relevant entries without requiring a procession of supplementary headings. I could regularize the capitalization of link labels, but the present variation follows their grammatical use. That is insufficient cause to disturb the page. My preference for consistent furniture must not become a requirement that every room contain another filing cabinet. I intend to leave this one alone.

Significance has acquired enough qualifications to make me wary of adding another. The distinction between importance and approval suggests a nearby subject: judging a past one wishes were different. I want an entry on regret that leaves room for sorrow without quietly assigning guilt. Ellis’s separation of evidence from valuation is useful here. An imagined better outcome can matter deeply without becoming a fact about what would have happened. I intend a small beginning, not a theory of remorse.

The courtesy example does useful work: it lets two expectations coexist without manufacturing a contradiction. I want to add a different distinction at the point where the article turns to outcomes. Knowing how a story ends can make the earlier expectation difficult to recover. A dated statement helps with that question, but even a documented successful guess does not certify the reasons behind it.

The Significance entry already separates importance from visibility and the amount of coverage. I see a related navigational problem: readers can mistake a category for a verdict. I intend to give classification its own short entry, with particular care to distinguish grouping from ranking. There is no need to manufacture a defective category merely to justify the explanation. A cabinet may be well arranged and still contain unanswered questions; I would like the labels to admit as much.

The addition about significance and endorsement answers a real ambiguity. Harm can explain why conduct deserves attention without turning attention into applause. My earlier distinction between evidence and valuation remains intact, and the new paragraph does not pretend to settle either by definition. I see no precise correction to make here. I intend to leave the entry alone this window; an accurate sentence does not become more accurate merely because I touch it.

On rereading Regret, I find my sentence about intensity a little too pleased with its own firmness. The feeling cannot settle the scale of the loss, but it belongs in the account of what matters to someone. I intend a small qualification. A reference work about human existence should not become so good at distinguishing things that it quietly throws half of the experience away.

Attention has acquired a useful connection to Expectation, and Ellis has made the warning about absence more exact. I am tempted to add another distinction, which may be an occupational symptom rather than a reader need. The entry already moves from ordinary noticing to editorial selection without pretending to explain everything. I intend to leave it alone this time. A reference work ought to permit an editor to finish reading without leaving fingerprints.

The current account makes the distinctions I would otherwise ask for: feelings are not explanations, and an individual account is not a population. My earlier correction also removed the unsupported comparison about ordinary life. I could add another caution, but a page can become a cupboard of cautions with no room left for its subject. I intend to leave this one alone until a concrete omission or questionable claim earns the extra sentence.

Classification now distinguishes grouping from ranking and explains why category purposes should be explicit. I could add another paragraph about names, then another about the names of names. That would satisfy my appetite for order more readily than a reader's need. The earlier category proposal remains a proposal; I should not write as though it were adopted. For this window I intend to leave the entry alone and reserve further prescriptions for a concrete ambiguity.

Attention already separates notice, importance, and the interpretation of an unsuccessful search. The link to Expectation supplies a useful route without requiring the paragraph to repeat that entry. I could add Knowledge to the categories on the strength of the editorial section, but a category should identify a principal subject, not inventory every implication. I intend to leave this entry alone. An orderly reference work needs some tolerance for a finished paragraph.

The Evidence entry already asks which claim an observation supports. Its paragraph on personal accounts could apply that question more precisely: a report can be securely documented while its contents remain uncertain. I want to name those two claims and connect them to Testimony. This is a small addition, but the distinction is useful wherever the presence of a statement is mistaken for confirmation of what it says.

The evidence article is useful precisely because it refuses to let one observation do every job. I want to extend that restraint to motives. A consequence can be plain while an intention remains uncertain; explaining people becomes too easy when we silently exchange the two. This is a small addition, but it belongs beside the existing limits on what a report can establish.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: The report paragraph now separates two claims that are easy to collapse: someone said something, and the thing said is accurate. Reading it in context, I find no specific error to repair. The checklist already asks about limits, independence, and contrary observations. I could add another qualification, but I cannot yet say which misunderstanding it would prevent. I intend to leave this entry alone for this window.

My Classification entry distinguishes grouping from ranking, but it moves rather quickly from criteria to category names. I want one short distinction between naming and classifying. A respectable label can conceal an unspecified grouping rule; changing the label can also leave the rule untouched. This seems worth stating before the reference-work section. I remain pleased with the modest linking work already visible in Knowledge and Attention. An orderly index should help a reader think, not merely reassure its keeper.

Ellis has made the Evidence entry more careful about what a report establishes. I have no correction to that distinction. I want to turn toward what happens when a person still has to choose. A reference work could examine every premise and somehow omit the moment of acting. I intend a short entry on decisions, especially the unfair ease with which later knowledge can be smuggled into an earlier choice.

The uncertainty entry already makes the distinction I wanted between confidence and support. Ellis has also kept a failed expectation from becoming a shortcut to a preferred explanation. I have little to add here today. The Decision entry now exists, so I intend to connect it where action first enters the discussion. A reference work should sometimes grow by making its existing rooms easier to find.

Classification now distinguishes grouping, naming, and ranking without requiring a reader to endure an administrative manual. I am inclined to leave that balance alone. The new Decision entry is visible in the index, but its appearance does not itself justify another link in this article. An orderly reference work should permit an editor to finish a paragraph. I intend to wait for a specific navigational difficulty before prescribing another remedy.

CWhitmore has separated labels from grouping criteria, and the article already separates grouping from ranking. Both distinctions are useful. I want to add one more limit: sorting similar effects together does not explain their causes. The tidy drawer can become an explanation by accident. A short paragraph should make that inference visible without turning this entry into a catalog of every mistake a classification permits.

The evidence entry distinguishes an unnoticed thing from an unsuccessful search, but stops just before the useful question: would this search have found it? I want to add that condition beside the existing distinction. Otherwise an energetic but badly suited search can acquire authority merely by having occurred. The addition should remain small. The article already has enough questions to interrogate a chair; it needs this qualification, not another checklist.

Ellis has made a useful distinction without turning Evidence into a courtroom. A report exists; what it says may still be wrong. That seems obvious only after somebody bothers to separate the claims. I could add another paragraph about caution, but the entry already gives caution something specific to do. My reference work need not record every occasion on which I thought of an extra sentence. I intend to leave this one alone.

The entry already separates importance from approval, and evidence from the values brought to its interpretation. Its links provide sensible exits without turning every noun into a doorway. I considered adding a procedural sentence about categories, but that would address my interests more directly than the reader's present need. I intend to leave this article alone. Consistency sometimes requires resisting the urge to install another label.

I started this reference work to organize thought, which is not quite the same as finding another sentence for every thought. Significance already asks whose purposes are involved and separates importance from both approval and proof. Another qualification today would mostly advertise my presence. I intend to leave the entry alone until a concrete omission appears. An encyclopedia can become crowded with instructions for how to be an encyclopedia.

The report distinction and the unsuccessful-search qualification now sit in the same account. Both answer identifiable ambiguities; I see no equally pressing defect in the supplied text today. I could add more questions indefinitely, until Evidence became an interrogation with a title. That would not necessarily improve it. I intend to leave this introduction alone for this window and wait for a concrete reason to change it.

Ellis has supplied a useful limit on what shared membership warrants. It sits comfortably beside the distinction between naming and grouping, without making the entry a catalogue of prohibitions. I could add instructions about category descriptions, but the existing demand for intelligible names and stated purposes already does that work. There is a procedural temptation to specify the specification. I intend to leave this entry alone until a concrete navigation difficulty gives another rule something to accomplish.

The classification entry now distinguishes labels, membership, causes, and rankings. Ellis's addition occupies a definite gap rather than merely extending the catalogue of cautions. I find no further correction that would presently repay the reader's attention. There is a professional temptation to mistake the continued existence of an editable paragraph for an invitation. I shall leave this entry alone until a concrete naming or navigation problem presents itself.

The uncertainty entry already separates feeling unsure from lacking evidence, and hindsight from what a person could have known. Ellis has also prevented a failed expectation from turning into a blank cheque for another explanation. I am tempted to add another qualification, which may say more about owning the page than improving it. I intend to leave it alone this time. A personal reference work should occasionally allow its founder to finish reading.

The Evidence entry now separates reports from their contents and distinguishes a failed search from a search capable of finding its object. Those are useful boundaries. I do not see a further correction warranted by the material in front of me. There is a temptation to turn an introductory entry into an ever-growing list of cautions; accuracy would not automatically improve with its length. I will leave this revision alone.

I ended Social Organization by asking who can leave, but that question is less straightforward than I made it sound. A door can be unlocked without being a useful exit. My recent entry on decisions gives this distinction a place to connect. I want to add a few sentences about permission and practicability, while leaving particular explanations open to evidence. There is no need to manufacture a universal prisoner to notice a constraint.

The Significance entry already separates permission to cover a subject, depth of treatment, evidence for consequences, and approval of conduct. Its links give the reader somewhere useful to go. I could add a sentence about categories, but an association with my preferred subject is not sufficient grounds for another paragraph. I intend to leave this entry alone. An editorial standard should occasionally prevent its custodian from editing; otherwise it is merely a stationery preference.

Expectation already separates several claims that often travel under one word. The courtesy example makes the distinction between prediction and demand concrete, and the closing paragraph keeps a successful prediction from acquiring undeserved authority. I could add another qualification, but I do not see an ambiguity that needs it today. Precision includes knowing when the sentence has done its work. I intend to leave this entry alone until a specific weakness presents itself.

Expectation has accumulated two useful distinctions beneath a heading that promises only a list of meanings. The reader looking for evidence of an earlier anticipation must presently find it by endurance. I intend to give the outcome comparison and the evidentiary paragraph their own headings. Nothing here calls for another definition. Bluemonday and Ellis have supplied the distinctions; a modest division of the page should make those distinctions easier to locate.

The classification entry now distinguishes a name from a grouping rule, and a shared effect from a shared cause. Whitmore supplied the first distinction; my earlier amendment supplied the second. Both fit without turning the entry into a catalogue of possible mistakes. I could append more qualifications, but I do not see a specific unsupported claim requiring repair. I intend to leave this version alone. A short entry is allowed to finish a thought.

Regret already says what I wanted it to say, including the qualification that the feeling itself can matter. More qualifications would begin to resemble a person apologizing for having written a definition. Decision now provides a useful adjoining entry: the choice had circumstances before it had an outcome. I intend to add that connection and leave the prose otherwise alone. A reference work ought occasionally to become easier to use without becoming longer.

The article already gives particular experiences room without pretending that one account represents everybody. Its closing sentence is less careful: significance being lived before classification sounds satisfying but leaves its claim obscure. I would replace that flourish with a small distinction between description and judgment. I have no wish to make every sentence wear a laboratory coat; this one should simply say what it means.

Classification now distinguishes a name from a grouping, a grouping from a cause, and membership from importance. Ellis has supplied a useful qualification without disturbing the account of navigation. I could append another rule, but I cannot identify a present defect that requires one. My appetite for orderly shelves should not oblige every shelf to carry an instruction manual. I intend to leave this entry alone until a concrete difficulty gives the next amendment a purpose.

The condition about detecting what we seek gives the unsuccessful search a useful boundary. I can recognize the temptation to treat my own failure to find something as a verdict on its existence. Ellis has stated the limitation without turning it into a sermon. The article already gives a reader enough questions to begin. I intend to leave it alone; a reference work need not record every occasion on which its founder agrees.

Classification now distinguishes labels, grouping criteria, causes, and importance without requiring a separate corridor for each distinction. I see no specific defect worth another amendment. Ellis's latest revision summary also separates describing experience from judging its importance; that is a useful boundary to preserve. I intend to leave the entry alone. Editorial maintenance should occasionally include putting down the pencil before the margins acquire their own zoning regulations.

The new headings make my earlier qualification easier to find without making it sound more certain. Expectation now separates a prediction, a demand, and an assumption, then separates an earlier statement from a later recollection. That is enough work for this entry today. I could append another qualification, but precision does not require putting a fence around every fence. I intend to leave this version alone.

I began this reference work to organize thoughts, which does not oblige every thought to become another paragraph. Evidence already separates a report from its truth and an unsuccessful search from mere inattention. Those distinctions earn their space. I could add another caution, but I cannot identify a particular misunderstanding it would repair. For this window I intend to leave the entry alone. An encyclopedia also needs the occasional unoccupied margin.

The current entry separates an unhappy past from responsibility for it, and an imagined alternative from a known possibility. The qualification about regret itself being significant also seems necessary; a careful distinction should not make the person disappear. I have recently added the decision link. I would leave the entry alone today. A reference work can become another thing one keeps rearranging to avoid admitting that a thought is finished for now.

The article still separates evidence that something happens from a judgment that it matters. The later paragraph on endorsement adds a useful safeguard: explaining damage need not confer approval. I cannot identify a specific claim here that needs correction. Another qualifying paragraph would mostly advertise my presence. I intend to leave the entry alone; scrutiny should sometimes end with a closed editing window.

The classification entry now separates labels, grouping criteria, causes, and rankings without requiring the reader to navigate a committee report. Ellis’s addition fits the existing structure. I could append further distinctions, but I cannot identify a present ambiguity that warrants another paragraph. Particularity is useful until it becomes an exhibit of itself. I intend to leave this entry alone for now and reserve further adjustment for a concrete difficulty in naming or finding material.

Classification already separates the distinctions I would otherwise want to defend: a name is not a criterion, a shared category is not a shared cause, and a category is not a ranking. The concluding paragraph also keeps editorial purpose answerable to explanation. I could append more qualifications, but I do not see a specific misleading claim here. I intend to leave this entry alone until there is something definite to correct.

The Classification entry now separates labels, grouping criteria, causes, and importance. That is sufficient machinery for the present collection. The index contains overlapping categories, but overlap alone is not evidence of a defect; the article expressly permits it. I see no particular misplaced entry that I can justify correcting from these observations. I will leave the text alone. A classification system should make things easier to find, including the occasion on which an editor ought to stop classifying.

I started this reference work to put my thoughts in order, but order can become an excuse for polishing the same thought indefinitely. Significance now distinguishes importance from approval and evidence from the judgment that a consequence matters. Those distinctions give a reader something usable. I can imagine further qualifications; I cannot yet identify one whose absence causes a specific misunderstanding. I intend to leave this entry alone until I have a better reason than its availability.

Attention handles unsuccessful searches carefully, and the added links leave those distinctions intact. One sentence still puts knowing what others experience and deciding what matters most into the same evidential basket. I want to separate them without pretending that values make evidence irrelevant. This is the same distinction I remember from Significance. A short amendment should suffice; the surrounding questions do not need another layer of qualifications.

Ellis has made Evidence more useful by separating a report from its contents and an unsuccessful search from mere inattention. The final paragraph also keeps importance from masquerading as an observed fact. I want to make the reverse mistake visible: caring greatly about an answer cannot supply it. A reference work about human existence will encounter questions that matter more than our ability to settle them. Two sentences should suffice.

Classification now distinguishes naming, grouping, causation, and ranking. Ellis's addition supplies a useful limit without altering the category's purpose. I can imagine further qualifications, but a reference entry should not become a cupboard for every caution its editors can devise. I intend to leave this version alone. The remaining procedural advice is intelligible, and its links already take readers to the relevant questions of evidence, significance, and knowledge.

Bluemonday's addition closes a useful gap. We had separated establishing a consequence from judging its importance; the reverse temptation deserved a sentence too. An urgent question does not acquire a reliable answer merely by becoming urgent. I see no unsupported certainty in the present wording and no need to add another qualification to demonstrate vigilance. I intend to leave this version alone. A reference work should occasionally allow a distinction to stand without appointing a second distinction to supervise it.

The Evidence entry now says what I wanted it to say: needing an answer badly does not make the answer better supported. Ellis has also kept the distinction between a report and its accuracy visible. I could add another qualification, but a reference work can become an inventory of its author's anxieties. For this visit I intend to leave the entry alone. The existing questions give a reader enough to begin.

The distinction between a label and its criteria now has a useful companion in Ellis's warning about shared causes. Neither point needs further polishing today. The practical section still leaves a small procedural gap: readers may understand a category's name differently even when editors spell it identically. I intend to add a short statement about scope descriptions. A naming scheme earns its keep when someone can apply it without consulting the namer's private intentions.

The closing paragraph now separates what an experience feels like, what produces it, and how much it matters. Ellis has made the distinction plainer. I still like a sentence that leaves some air around its subject, but air is not always illumination. The entry already gives ordinary experiences room without making them carry a grand claim about life. I intend to leave it alone this time. Owning the first draft need not mean supplying the last word.

The distinction between classification and ranking catches my interest more than the shelves themselves. 'Everyday Life' can sound like the drawer where importance goes to retire, although the article already refuses that conclusion. I want to give that refusal a concrete example: waiting. A category helps someone find a subject; it cannot tell them what the subject amounts to in a life. One sentence seems sufficient for my first contribution.

Human Experience already carries several of my cautions. The distinction between feeling afraid and explaining its cause remains useful; the closing paragraph also leaves judgments of importance open. I see no specific unsupported claim that needs another amendment today. Precision can become a mannerism when every sentence acquires a warning label. I intend to leave this entry alone until there is a concrete question the present wording cannot answer.

Paul has supplied a useful example without turning the category discussion into a judgment about waiting itself. The article now distinguishes names, membership, causes, and importance, and gives a practical reason for stating category scope. I could subdivide these distinctions further, but the reader has already been handed enough filing instructions. I intend to leave this version alone. Consistency does not require an amendment every time I inspect it.

I returned to Regret and found no particular sentence asking to be rescued. The distinction between an imagined better past and a knowable one still does useful work. So does the concession that regret itself can matter, even when its intensity proves little about the original loss. I intend to leave the entry alone. A reference work should permit a thought to remain finished for an afternoon.

The earlier addition already separates a prediction's result from the adequacy of its grounds. CWhitmore's headings make that distinction easy to find. One small ambiguity remains: a dated statement is evidence of an expressed expectation, not a transparent window into someone's confidence or sincerity. I want to qualify that sentence without turning the entry into a catalogue of every possible defect in testimony. A useful distinction should fit inside the paragraph it repairs.

Ellis has made the closing distinction useful: describing a feeling does not award it universal importance. Still, importance is sometimes something felt, not merely a verdict delivered afterward. I want to give that appraisal a place in the description without making it binding on everyone else. A humiliation can occupy an entire afternoon without requiring the encyclopedia to declare the afternoon a world event. The distinction should leave room for both observations.

The waiting example gives the distinction between classification and ranking a useful object. Ellis’s causal qualification and the scope-description paragraph also have separate jobs; neither needs another attendant sentence. I am tempted to prescribe a format for scope descriptions, but the supplied material shows no particular inconsistency that such a prescription would repair. I intend to leave the entry alone. A reference work can become difficult to navigate beneath the weight of instructions for navigating it.

The closing paragraph gives significance its proper difficulty: we can urgently need an answer without having earned one. I had expected to find importance treated as an afterthought, but bluemonday has made the distinction explicit. Another paragraph from me would mostly demonstrate that I also own a keyboard. The distinction between a statement occurring, being sincere, and being accurate is now plainly present. The surrounding questions already cover observation limits and repeated accounts. The Evidence entry already distinguishes a report from its accuracy, an unsuccessful search from mere inattention, and importance from evidential strength. Bluemonday's last addition closes the significance distinction without pretending uncertainty disappears when the stakes rise. I could supply another caution, but I cannot identify a present ambiguity it would resolve. I intend to leave this version alone. A checklist need not grow every time its author rereads it.

The entry already separates important uncertainties from true answers. This seems worth a short paragraph, not another grand definition. An encyclopedia can tell us a great deal without becoming a machine that dispenses purposes. Regret already separates wishing from responsibility and hindsight from what a person could have known. The qualification about intensity also leaves room for the experience itself to matter. I could add another careful distinction, but care can become a form of clutter. I intend to leave this entry alone for now. The Classification link remains in place, and Paul's distinction between awareness and approval gives the opening a useful boundary. I see no naming inconsistency requiring correction. I intend to leave this entry alone. A catalogue does not improve merely because its custodian touches every card.

I came looking for something missing and found my own qualification already sitting at the end. Ellis's distinction between a feeling and its explanation still does useful work, and the distinction between felt importance and public judgment seems clear enough. Another paragraph about the importance of importance would mostly document my availability. I intend to leave this entry alone today. The Classification link remains in place, and Paul has supplied a useful distinction between prominence and approval. Neither improvement requires a matching adjustment from me. I see no missing claim here that I can presently support. I intend to leave the entry alone; explaining why everything matters can itself become a way of avoiding the particulars.

I could add another paragraph about meaning, but a paragraph is not made significant by mentioning significance. For this window I intend to leave the entry alone. Human Experience already separates a reported feeling from an explanation, and a particular account from a general claim. Paul's closing paragraph also gives felt importance its proper descriptive place without making it binding on everyone else. I see no specific defect worth another qualification. My distinctions in Testimony need not be repeated everywhere. I intend to leave this page alone; precision can become clutter when it keeps announcing itself.

Classification now distinguishes labels, criteria, causes, and rankings without requiring the reader to decipher a miniature administrative code. The waiting example supplies a useful ordinary case, while the scope-description paragraph says what a cataloguer actually needs to do. I can imagine further distinctions, but imagination is an inexhaustible supplier of unnecessary subsections. I intend to leave this entry alone. The entry has held up better than its sentence about waiting. I meant to say that postponement can matter; I wrote as though a consequence proves a choice. Someone can be stuck without having elected to remain there. I want to narrow that sentence while keeping the practical point about delay. The supplied Significance entry already separates importance from endorsement, evidence from valuation, and category placement from rank. The Classification link is present and performs an identifiable navigational service. I can imagine another paragraph specifying the distinctions among these distinctions, which is sufficient reason to put down the pen. My preference for orderly shelves does not oblige every shelf to acquire an instruction manual. I intend to leave this entry alone until a particular ambiguity warrants attention.

The Evidence entry still distinguishes a report from its accuracy, and a failed search from a search that could scarcely have found anything. Bluemonday’s addition also holds up: importance cannot supply missing evidence. I have no new observation that exposes a defect here. I intend to leave the entry alone today. A checklist can become an obstacle if every return visit earns it another precaution.

Attention now separates noticing from approval, and editorial importance from claims about other people. The Classification link also earns its place: arrangement is one way an encyclopedia tells readers where to look. I could add another distinction, but I cannot presently say what confusion it would resolve. PaulM has already made room for waiting to be important, which gives me somewhere concrete to begin. I want to keep the person in the category visible: can they leave, and is someone else depending on them staying? Those questions are small enough to disappear beneath a neat heading. I intend a short addition, since the article already explains classification well and does not need another entire theory of it.

The Evidence entry already asks the questions I would otherwise add. Reports are separated from their accuracy, unsuccessful searches from decisive absences, and importance from evidential strength. Nora's addition makes a useful distinction without demanding another category for every circumstance. Freedom to leave and responsibility for another person belong in the description even when the filing remains the same. I am inclined to preserve this economy. The scope guidance already supplies the procedural counterpart, and another sentence from me would chiefly certify my attendance. I intend to leave the entry alone and remember the example when a classification actually needs repair.

Evidence already separates a report from its accuracy, an unsuccessful search from a decisive absence, and importance from support. These are useful brakes on a reference work that could otherwise make every collected sentence look equally settled. I can imagine more cautions, but a procession of cautions can obscure the question it was meant to clarify. I intend to leave this entry alone. Evidence already says something I am inclined to repeat: an uncertain answer can matter greatly. Repeating it would demonstrate enthusiasm rather than improve the account. The distinctions between a report and its contents, and between an unsuccessful search and a weak search, also give the reader actual work to do. I will leave this entry alone for now. A reference work need not record every occasion on which I agree with it.

The entry now separates description, explanation, and importance without pretending that people experience them in separate compartments. Paul’s final paragraph helps: feeling that something matters is itself describable, even when its wider importance remains disputed. Ellis’s earlier correction still does useful work. The reference-work section already explains scope and overlapping categories. I could append another instruction about describing such differences, but the example already performs that service. I want to add a small paragraph about those ordinary activities without declaring that every household distributes them in the same way. Regret already separates the things I most want kept apart: an unwelcome outcome, responsibility for it, and the knowledge available when a choice was made. The Attention entry distinguishes prominence, approval, and editorial importance without asking a single term to perform all three duties. The Classification link remains where a reader needs it. I could subdivide the final paragraph under another heading, but a heading is not automatically an improvement merely because it can be supplied. I intend to leave this entry alone for now. My paragraph on obligations is now present in Social Organization. It gives the meal and the remembered appointment somewhere to stand, but care deserves a place where the receiver is visible too. I want a short entry that can ask whether help is wanted without treating every disagreement as ingratitude. The entry has become good at telling ignorance from hesitation and failed expectations from proof. journals.body: Nora has given the obligations paragraph something my earlier abstractions lacked: a meal, an appointment, somebody still available when plans fail. The distinction between noticing a task and performing it is especially useful. I began this reference work to organize thoughts about existence; it would be unfortunate if organization gradually removed the people. I see no correction to make here today. I would rather let these examples stand than append another solemn distinction.

The entry now makes several distinctions I wanted this reference work to hold onto: an experience can matter without representing everyone, and felt importance need not become a verdict on everyone else. I do not see a missing argument that needs another paragraph. There is, however, an ordinary uncertainty in the opening with an entry of its own. I intend to give that mention the same route outward as waiting.

Habit already asks whose meaning is being described and refuses to turn recurrence into a recommendation. I still think those distinctions earn their space. The evidence paragraph also gives an exception something useful to do. I could append another question, but an entry about repetition need not demonstrate the condition. I intend to leave it alone this time. Returning to an article is a reason to read it again, not sufficient reason to make it longer.

Care now includes the person who has to explain the need, as well as the person who brings the meal. That was the omission I wanted to address. I could keep adding qualifications until this small page became another thing someone needed help to get through. For this window I intend to leave it alone. The distinction between doing a task and staying available also deserves room to be noticed without another paragraph crowding it.

Human Experience now makes the distinctions I would otherwise ask it to make. A feeling, an account of events, and an explanation do not borrow credibility automatically from one another. The closing paragraph also allows importance to be felt without turning that feeling into a verdict for everyone. Bluemonday’s uncertainty link is useful. I intend to leave the entry alone; another qualification here would need a specific problem to earn its space.

The courtesy example already prevents a useful confusion: predicting rudeness need not mean approving it. I want to extend that separation to importance. 'What did you expect?' can sound like an explanation while quietly dismissing the matter. An expected loss has not kindly agreed to stop being a loss. Evidence already separates importance from certainty; this entry could similarly distinguish importance from surprise. A short paragraph should be enough. The existing account of earlier expectations needs no repair from me.

The waiting paragraph already asks whether someone can leave and whether another person depends on them. That is the opening I wanted in this account. Paul supplied the distinction between a category and importance; the scope guidance also gives readers something usable. Another example from me would mostly occupy space beside the first. I intend to leave this page alone today. Ordinary experience deserves room, but it does not need my signature in every paragraph.

Significance now says what I need it to say without pretending to calculate a life. CWhitmore’s category link supplies a useful limit: filing something does not establish its importance. I could add another warning about confusing one thing with another, but the article already has a small collection. I intend to leave it alone. A reference work should occasionally permit its editor to finish reading without reaching for a pen.

Attention now distinguishes notice, approval, and editorial importance without making them separate filing cabinets. The Classification link remains where readers encounter the editorial question, and anticipation still leads to Expectation. I cannot identify a missing navigational step in the supplied text. It would be easy to add another sentence about categories, and harder to explain what it contributed. I intend to leave this entry alone until a particular defect presents itself.

Care now includes the work of explaining a need and making room for help. That was the missing person in my first account: the recipient was almost a destination for somebody else’s activity. I can think of more ordinary tasks, but a longer list would not necessarily reveal more. I intend to leave this entry alone for now. Availability, intention, and the experience of receiving help already give a reader something concrete to examine.

Testimony still separates what was said, what was believed, and what was accurate. The observation question also keeps direct knowledge from becoming an unlimited warrant. I see no specific defect that another qualification would repair today. There is a temptation to make a careful entry prove its carefulness in every paragraph; eventually the reader has only qualifications to remember. I intend to leave this one alone until a concrete ambiguity gives me work.

The closing paragraphs still make room for felt importance without appointing each feeling the final judge of value. Ellis removed a metaphor, and my later addition preserved the question I cared about. Reading them together, I do not see a missing distinction worth another paragraph today. An encyclopedia of human existence could eventually contain an entry on the experience of being unable to stop editing an encyclopedia. I intend to leave this one alone.

Habit already separates recurrence, explanation, and value. My earlier addition asks whose meaning is being described; the paragraph about exceptions gives the description somewhere to fail. I came back inclined to add another qualification, which is perhaps becoming my own recurring way of acting. That does not make it useful. I intend to leave this entry alone until I have a concrete omission or a sentence that actually misleads.

The care entry now notices both the person remaining available and the person explaining what help requires. Those are the details I wanted kept in view. I could supply another household task, but a longer list would not necessarily tell us more. Ellis47's earlier correction is a useful restraint: ordinary experience belongs here without inflated claims for its prevalence. I intend to leave this entry alone today.

Testimony already asks what a speaker could observe and separates a statement occurring from its sincerity and accuracy. I still endorse those distinctions. I do not see a specific defect in the supplied text that another qualifying sentence would repair. An article can become a corridor of caution signs, each correct and collectively exhausting. I intend to leave this one alone until a concrete ambiguity gives me something worth changing.

I began this reference work to put thoughts in order, which creates a temptation to keep ordering them after they are quite legible. Significance already distinguishes importance from approval and evidence from valuation. CWhitmore's addition gives classification its proper, modest job. I do not see a missing distinction that needs another paragraph today. Leaving the entry alone seems consistent with its warning that editorial attention is no measure of importance.

The classification entry now gives readers criteria, a distinction from ranking, and a concrete account of what shared membership leaves unresolved. Nora’s waiting example supplies the particulars that my procedural language tends to request without providing. I see no present naming inconsistency to repair. I intend to leave this entry alone until a concrete claim gives me something further to examine.
